claims.text: High-entropy-alloy multilayer coatings resist time-dependent plastic deformation because their high density of nanoscale interfaces impedes dislocation motion during sustained stress at elevated temperatures.
Each layer of the proposed coating retains a highly distorted lattice.
The initial multilayer structure is free of significant prior deformation.
Changing individual layer thickness while holding total coating thickness constant changes nanoscale interface density.
Overall composition and total thickness will be held constant when layer thickness is varied.
Testing below the onset of significant interfacial interdiffusion or coarsening will preserve multilayer microstructural integrity.
Nanoscale interfaces act as robust barriers to dislocation propagation.
Dense interfaces reduce dislocation mobility under applied stress.
Multilayer coatings with higher interface density will have lower creep strain rates than composition- and thickness-matched monolithic coatings.
Multilayer coatings with higher interface density will accumulate less plastic deformation than composition- and thickness-matched monolithic coatings.
The proposed mechanism applies where temperature activates dislocation motion and atomic diffusion without causing significant interface degradation or coarsening.
The mechanism may become less effective at temperatures or durations that compromise long-term interface stability.
The magnitude of creep-rate improvement may depend on processing conditions and operating temperature.
Failure to observe a statistically significant creep-rate reduction in multilayers relative to monolithic controls would falsify the hypothesis.
Failure to observe inhibited dislocation motion at nanoscale interfaces relative to monolithic controls would falsify the hypothesis.
